passage:
The mantis shrimp, a marine crustacean found chiefly in tropical and subtropical shallow waters, possesses one of the most remarkable visual systems known to science. Where the human eye relies on three types of photoreceptor cells sensitive to different wavelengths of light — giving rise to what is commonly described as trichromatic vision — the mantis shrimp retina contains sixteen distinct receptor types. For decades, researchers assumed this arrangement granted the animal a correspondingly richer subjective experience of color, a form of hyperspectral vision that would allow it to discriminate among hues invisible to any other creature.

However, subsequent behavioral research has cast serious doubt on this assumption. In a series of carefully controlled experiments, investigators trained mantis shrimp to associate specific wavelengths of light with a food reward and then tested their ability to discriminate between wavelengths separated by progressively smaller intervals. Surprisingly, the animals performed markedly worse at fine spectral discrimination than would be predicted by the number of their receptor types — and, in some trials, no better than humans. The standard model of color vision holds that more receptor types translate directly into finer wavelength discrimination, because each additional receptor provides a comparison signal that narrows the range of confusion. The mantis shrimp data appear to violate this relationship.

The leading alternative hypothesis proposes that the mantis shrimp visual system operates not by spectral comparison — the mechanism underlying human color vision — but by a process closer to wavelength labeling. According to this account, each receptor class is tuned to a narrow, largely non-overlapping band of the spectrum, and the nervous system reads the identity of whichever receptor fires most strongly rather than computing a ratio across receptors. This would make color recognition extremely fast and computationally inexpensive, trading fine discrimination for speed. Proponents of the labeling hypothesis note that mantis shrimp are highly territorial predators that must make near-instantaneous decisions about approaching rivals or prey; rapid classification of a stimulus, even at coarse resolution, may confer a greater survival advantage than the slow, precise comparisons that trichromatic vision affords.

Nonetheless, important questions remain. Laboratory experiments necessarily reduce the complexity of natural visual environments, and it is possible that the full sixteen-receptor system reveals advantages not captured by wavelength-discrimination tasks alone — sensitivity to polarized light, for instance, or the detection of specific biological signals on the bodies of conspecifics. The debate illustrates a broader challenge in sensory ecology: the architecture of a sensory system cannot be read straightforwardly as a measure of the richness of the experience it produces. Function, as the mantis shrimp case suggests, may be better understood by asking what decisions the system enables rather than how faithfully it reproduces the physical world.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mantis shrimp's sixteen photoreceptor types give it a richer subjective experience of color than any other known animal possesses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Behavioral evidence suggests that the mantis shrimp visual system operates by a labeling mechanism rather than spectral comparison, complicating the assumption that more receptors yield finer discrimination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory experiments have conclusively demonstrated that the mantis shrimp cannot discriminate among wavelengths as well as humans can.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chief purpose of the mantis shrimp's unusual retina is to detect polarized light and biological signals on the bodies of rivals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Understanding the mantis shrimp visual system requires abandoning all existing models of color vision and developing entirely new theoretical frameworks.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the assumption that more receptors yield finer discrimination, presents behavioral evidence undermining it, and proposes the labeling hypothesis as an alternative — while noting remaining questions. Choice B integrates these strands accurately.
explanations.A: This restates the initial assumption that the passage then challenges; it is the view the passage argues against, not its main point.
explanations.B: Correct. This captures both the evidential challenge to the standard model and the alternative hypothesis, which together constitute the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Too strong and too narrow: the passage says mantis shrimp performed 'no better than humans' in some trials, not conclusively worse in all tasks, and this is one finding rather than the main point.
explanations.D: This is mentioned only as a possibility in the final paragraph; the passage does not assert it as the 'chief purpose' of the retina.
explanations.E: The passage does not call for abandoning all existing models; it proposes a specific alternative mechanism and notes remaining questions. This overstates the author's position.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A widely held hypothesis is introduced; behavioral evidence is presented that challenges it; an alternative hypothesis is offered; remaining questions are noted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A new discovery is announced; its implications for human medicine are explored; a competing theory is refuted; a practical application is recommended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing hypotheses are introduced simultaneously; experimental data supporting each are described; the author endorses one; open questions are dismissed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A phenomenon is described; its historical origins are traced; a series of experiments is summarized; a definitive conclusion is reached.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An assumption is challenged by new data; a refinement of that assumption is offered; an unrelated finding is introduced; the passage ends with a policy recommendation.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces the hyperspectral-vision assumption; paragraph 2 presents behavioral evidence challenging it; paragraph 3 proposes the labeling hypothesis; paragraph 4 notes remaining questions and a broader implication. Choice A maps directly onto this four-paragraph structure.
explanations.B: Human medicine is never mentioned, and no practical application is recommended — this choice invents moves the passage never makes.
explanations.C: The two hypotheses are not introduced simultaneously; the alternative is presented only after the standard model is challenged. Nor does the author definitively endorse one, and open questions are not dismissed.
explanations.D: The passage does not trace historical origins, and it does not reach a definitive conclusion — the final paragraph explicitly flags remaining uncertainty.
explanations.E: The passage does not introduce an unrelated finding, and it ends with a general observation about sensory ecology, not a policy recommendation.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the standard model of color vision predicts that animals with more photoreceptor types should

choices.label: A
choices.text: process visual information more slowly than animals with fewer receptor types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: rely on wavelength labeling rather than spectral comparison.

choices.label: C
choices.text: be capable of finer discrimination among wavelengths of light.

choices.label: D
choices.text: detect polarized light more readily than trichromatic animals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: perform better than trichromatic animals only when distinguishing colors at the extreme ends of the visible spectrum.

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly: 'The standard model of color vision holds that more receptor types translate directly into finer wavelength discrimination, because each additional receptor provides a comparison signal that narrows the range of confusion.'
explanations.A: The standard model says nothing about processing speed; that concern belongs to the labeling hypothesis, which trades precision for speed.
explanations.B: Wavelength labeling is the alternative hypothesis that the standard model does not predict; it is what the mantis shrimp data appear to suggest instead.
explanations.C: Correct. This is a direct paraphrase of the passage's statement of the standard model.
explanations.D: Polarized-light detection is mentioned only in the final paragraph as a possible advantage not captured by discrimination tasks; it is not part of the standard model.
explanations.E: The standard model makes no claim about performance only at the spectral extremes; this qualifier is not supported by the passage.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that proponents of the wavelength-labeling hypothesis would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Having a greater number of photoreceptor types is always disadvantageous for an animal that relies on rapid predation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The survival value of a visual system depends in part on the speed with which it can classify stimuli.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trichromatic animals are generally better hunters than those with more receptor types.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The mantis shrimp's visual system should be regarded as defective because it fails to achieve fine spectral discrimination.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The labeling mechanism evolved specifically as a response to the loss of spectral comparison ability in an ancestor of the mantis shrimp.

explanations.correct: The passage states that proponents of the labeling hypothesis note mantis shrimp 'must make near-instantaneous decisions' and that 'rapid classification…may confer a greater survival advantage than the slow, precise comparisons that trichromatic vision affords.' This directly implies that speed of classification has survival value.
explanations.A: Too strong: proponents argue that labeling trades precision for speed as an advantage in this ecological context, not that more receptors are 'always' disadvantageous. The absolute qualifier makes this incorrect.
explanations.B: Correct. The labeling hypothesis specifically invokes speed-of-classification as the adaptive benefit, implying that survival value is partly a function of stimulus-classification speed.
explanations.C: The passage makes no comparative claim about trichromatic animals as hunters; this goes beyond what the labeling hypothesis entails.
explanations.D: Proponents of labeling treat the low discrimination scores as consistent with an adaptive mechanism, not as a defect — the opposite of this choice.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing about the evolutionary history of the mantis shrimp visual system; this is outside the scope of what the labeling hypothesis claims.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of polarized light and biological signals in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide a definitive explanation for why the mantis shrimp requires sixteen receptor types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a new hypothesis that supersedes the wavelength-labeling account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: suggest that laboratory discrimination tasks may not capture all the functional advantages conferred by the mantis shrimp's visual system.

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the behavioral experiments described in the second paragraph were methodologically flawed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast the mantis shrimp's visual abilities with those of humans in low-light environments.

explanations.correct: The final paragraph notes 'it is possible that the full sixteen-receptor system reveals advantages not captured by wavelength-discrimination tasks alone — sensitivity to polarized light, for instance.' This functions to qualify the scope of the behavioral experiments and preserve uncertainty about the full utility of the system.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly does not provide a definitive explanation — it presents this as a possibility using 'it is possible that.' This choice overstates the passage's claim.
explanations.B: Polarized-light sensitivity is raised as an unresolved possibility, not as a new competing hypothesis that replaces the labeling account.
explanations.C: Correct. The mention of polarized light and biological signals qualifies the experimental evidence by pointing to potential adaptive functions that discrimination tasks would not reveal.
explanations.D: The passage does not characterize the experiments as flawed; it merely notes their limited scope. There is a difference between methodological limitation and methodological flaw.
explanations.E: Low-light environments are never mentioned; this choice fabricates a comparison that does not appear in the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the wavelength-labeling hypothesis can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, as the author treats the labeling hypothesis as having resolved the problem the behavioral experiments raised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious interest, as the author presents it as a plausible account consistent with the behavioral data but acknowledges that important questions remain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: mild skepticism, as the author implies the labeling hypothesis is less well supported by evidence than the standard model it seeks to replace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright dismissal, as the author indicates the labeling hypothesis fails to account for the mantis shrimp's poor discrimination scores.

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral indifference, as the author declines to evaluate either hypothesis and simply presents facts about the mantis shrimp retina.

explanations.correct: The author presents the labeling hypothesis substantively and approvingly — explaining its logic and the adaptive rationale offered by its proponents — but the final paragraph explicitly notes that 'important questions remain' and that laboratory tasks may not capture all relevant variables. This combination reflects cautious interest rather than endorsement or skepticism.
explanations.A: Overstates the author's stance: the passage's final paragraph carefully hedges with remaining questions and the phrase 'it is possible.' The problem is not treated as resolved.
explanations.B: Correct. The author explains the labeling hypothesis sympathetically and notes its adaptive logic, while the final paragraph preserves uncertainty.
explanations.C: The passage does not imply the labeling hypothesis is less well supported; if anything, the behavioral data are more consistent with labeling than with the standard model.
explanations.D: The author never dismisses the labeling hypothesis; on the contrary, it is the account the author spends most of paragraph 3 expounding.
explanations.E: The author is not neutrally indifferent — the final paragraph's editorial observation ('Function…may be better understood by asking what decisions the system enables') signals active engagement and a perspective.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the wavelength-labeling hypothesis as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mantis shrimp were found to have reaction times to visual stimuli significantly faster than those of other crustaceans with fewer receptor types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Analysis of the mantis shrimp nervous system revealed that signals from different receptor types are extensively compared before reaching the brain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A study showed that mantis shrimp are capable of discriminating among wavelengths separated by intervals as small as one nanometer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researchers discovered that the sixteen receptor types of the mantis shrimp overlap substantially in the wavelengths to which they are sensitive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: New evidence indicated that the mantis shrimp's poor performance on discrimination tasks was caused by a failure to understand the experimental instructions.

explanations.correct: The labeling hypothesis proposes that the system trades fine discrimination for speed, providing rapid stimulus classification as an adaptive advantage. Evidence that mantis shrimp respond to visual stimuli faster than comparable crustaceans would directly support the speed-advantage component of the hypothesis.
explanations.A: Correct. This evidence supports the core claim that the labeling mechanism enables faster processing — the adaptive benefit the hypothesis invokes to explain why the system sacrifices fine discrimination.
explanations.B: If receptor signals are extensively compared before reaching the brain, that would resemble spectral comparison, the mechanism of the standard model — this would weaken, not strengthen, the labeling hypothesis.
explanations.C: Fine nanometer-scale discrimination would support the standard model's prediction, directly contradicting the behavioral evidence that motivates the labeling hypothesis.
explanations.D: Substantial overlap among receptor types would undermine the labeling hypothesis, which specifically requires that each receptor be 'tuned to a narrow, largely non-overlapping band' to enable clean identity-based labeling.
explanations.E: This would suggest the experimental results are artifactual and tell us nothing about the mantis shrimp's actual visual mechanism; it neither strengthens nor meaningfully engages the labeling hypothesis as a mechanistic account.
